name: Uma Olsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers or AI firms. This is confidential. What's a usual workday like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I teach percussion on Thursdays, record at Harbour Studio twice a month, and lead a small ensemble when venues call. I have a master's in music and use AI every day for practice notes, but listening to another player is still the best part.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How steady is the work right now?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The pay is fairly typical for this job, and there are some other music jobs nearby. I have about three months of expenses saved, though a long quiet winter would eat it.

say: I'd say **live rehearsal** and playing still earn their place.
I'd welcome **faster paperwork** because it gives me another hour to practise.
think: My **three-month reserve** covers a cancelled date, but repeated gaps would hurt.
The studio's **winter calendar** is the uncertainty I already watch.
do: Keep my **Thursday pupils** and two monthly studio sessions.
Transfer **one hundred** from each cleared studio fee to savings.
feel: I feel **settled** about my work, though I watch the booking calendar.
S0.quote: A cancelled studio date stings; three empty months would change the picture.
fieldNote: Her **moderate cushion** lets her absorb one moved session without losing rent money.
She uses **AI daily** for notes, but a plateau changes little about her performing income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the ensemble that tidy invoices are welcome, but people still need us to rehearse and play. I already use AI to sort practice notes, and it saves me an hour on Mondays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My three months of savings mean one lost recording session would sting, not sink me. I still wonder if the studio will book enough winter work; that's the usual worry, not a new machine fear. A cancelled studio date stings; three empty months would change the picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep my Thursday teaching block and the two monthly percussion sessions at Harbour Studio. Starting this month, I'll move a hundred from each studio fee into savings when it clears, and keep doing that through the year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel fairly settled about the work, with one eye on the studio calendar. A quiet winter is possible, but I have time to find another booking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened the last time a studio date moved?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The studio cancelled one date in March and moved it to May. My teaching income covered the gap, so I didn't have to touch savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you handle a clash between jobs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the studio producer for dates in writing before accepting a conflicting school workshop. I'd rather know early than guess which cheque will land.

I'd show bookers the value of **responsive playing** in the room.

Postpone the **drum set** if the editing work disappears.
feel: I feel **anxious** about income, curious about a small class test.
S1.quote: Twelve paid places matter more than twelve people clicking interested.
fieldNote: She names the **one-third exposure** in editing rather than treating all music work alike.
Her **paid-place threshold** protects the three-month reserve from a room-fee loss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my students to learn the tools and still learn how to listen. Studios may use generated scores, but a drummer who can respond to a singer is worth bringing in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The arranging and track-cleaning jobs could fall quickly, and those are about a third of my income. I can teach and play live, yet the studio may stop calling for small edits before robots touch instruments.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'll record three short examples of musicians changing a groove together and show them to two venue bookers. If edit fees drop in the first year, I'll offer a paid group rhythm class at the college, but only if twelve people enrol and the room fee is covered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about a third of my pay, and curious about what I can build. Three months of savings buys a test, not a whole new career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would losing editing pay change first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last quarter I earned about nine hundred from cleaning tracks and preparing arrangements. If that went, I'd postpone the new drum set and use the old kit another year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What makes the group class worth trying?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would price the class before advertising it. The college charges for the room, so twelve paid places is my minimum, not twelve people clicking interested. Twelve paid places matter more than twelve people clicking interested.

I'd say **live work** has time until robots arrive around 2031.
think: **AGI in 2028** threatens my arranging and editing income first.
My **three-month reserve** could shrink before any robot plays a drum.
do: Split twelve months of **income records** into live, teaching and screen work now.
Seek **two college teaching days** after 2028 if studio edit fees halve.
Apply to **three music schools** if the college cannot offer those days.
feel: I feel **anxious** about a sharp income cut, with time and nearby schools to try.
S2.quote: My kit can stay on stage while my invoices disappear.
fieldNote: Her **live work** may outlast screen work by three years in this scenario.
She keeps **new equipment spending** conditional on signed teaching work, protecting savings.

steps.text: Seek two college teaching days after 2028 if edit fees halve

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the ensemble the 2028 deadline is close enough to check every contract now. We should hold on to the rights to our recordings and keep playing together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2028, AGI could do my arranging, editing and teaching plans for less than I charge. Robots reaching hands-on playing about 2031 gives live work another three years, but losing a third of my pay first would burn through savings fast. My kit can stay on stage while my invoices disappear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'll separate my last twelve months of income into live, teaching and screen work, then ask the college about more ensemble lessons. In the first year after 2028, if studio editing fees halve, I'll take two additional teaching days if the college offers them; otherwise I'll apply to three nearby music schools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious, not frozen, because three months of expenses and some nearby jobs give me a route to try. I would still hate watching the editing part of my craft become a button.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What exactly would you ask the college for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I won't ask the college to promise hours it cannot fund. I'd ask for its next term timetable and apply elsewhere while it decides.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the new classes require expensive equipment?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can teach percussion groups with the kit I already own. I wouldn't buy more instruments until a school signs for the extra classes.

say: I'd say **five years** gives us time to build listeners and group teaching.
I'd keep testing **live formats** before studio edit calls fade.
think: **AGI in 2031** could replace arranging before robots reach stages around 2034.
The **five-year window** lets me shift income, though ordinary AI may erode edits earlier.
do: Pitch a **six-week course** next term with a guaranteed college fee.
Aim for **half my pay** from teaching and live groups by 2031.
Add a **second course** after AGI only if the first brings repeat pupils.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about studio fees, with room to test a course safely.
S3.quote: An empty class is the college's risk only if the fee is written down.
fieldNote: She uses the **five-year window** to change income composition before AGI arrives.
A **guaranteed teaching fee** and repeat enrolment determine whether she expands without spending her three-month reserve.
Her **edit income** faces ordinary AI erosion before 2031, making her own income realistically vulnerable despite measured delivery.

steps.text: Pitch a six-week ensemble course with a guaranteed college fee

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the ensemble five years gives us time to build listeners, not permission to relax. I would try new formats before the studio calls stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AGI in 2031 would still make my arranging and lesson plans cheap, and robot players could reach stages around 2034. With five years, I could shift toward teaching people to play together, though the studio's editing fees may erode earlier under ordinary AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting next term, I'll pitch a six-week ensemble course to the college and run it only if the college guarantees the teaching fee. By 2031 I'll aim to have half my income from teaching and live groups; in the first year after AGI, I'll drop edit work that no longer pays and add a second course only if the first has repeat enrolment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about losing studio tasks, but I can make a measured change over five years. I don't need to spend my whole reserve on one experiment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who pays if too few people enrol?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The college already has drums and a rehearsal room. I'd ask for a fixed fee per six-week course, so I don't take the whole risk of empty seats. An empty class is the college's risk only if the fee is written down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would tell you not to repeat the course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the first course finishes without enough repeat pupils, I won't book a second one. I'd take more venue dates and ask another college about group teaching.

I'd use **ten years** to grow teaching before the studio work fades.
think: At **37**, I would still need a long career when AGI arrives in 2036.
Robot performers around **2039** could reach stages, so a paid teaching programme matters.

S4.quote: I won't put a hall deposit on my card to prove the future of music.
fieldNote: Her **sponsor condition** keeps a long-range idea from draining today's reserve.
She measures success by **paid term pupils**, not applause at a one-day event or social media interest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell students ten years is enough time to learn new ways of making music without giving up the stage. I would show them the software and still ask them to play together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 37 in 2036, I will need decades of income beyond AGI, and robot performers might follow around 2039. A decade gives me a chance to build a teaching programme and keep playing, although the recording work could thin out earlier.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next year I'll test a yearly community percussion day with the college if a sponsor covers the hall and player fees. Across the decade I'll grow my savings to six months of expenses from paid classes; in the first year after 2036, I'll keep the event only if it still brings paid pupils into the programme.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel hopeful about having ten years, and still practical about today's bookings. I can plan a programme without pretending every experiment will work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you refuse to pay for up front?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The college can lend instruments, but I would not put a hall deposit on my card. I'd get the sponsor agreement and the college room confirmation before selling places. I won't put a hall deposit on my card to prove the future of music.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you judge whether the event worked?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The event only matters if people return for lessons. I'd count how many pay for a term afterward, then decide whether next year's day is worth the work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the arranging and editing fees could go before I have time to replace them. A guaranteed college teaching fee and clear recording rights would let me shift without spending the reserve on guesses.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what pupils get from making music together. They learn to hear and respond to another person, and I want to know whether families will keep paying for that.

headlineQuote: Three months of savings buys a test, not a whole new career.
portrait: Uma is a **27-year-old** percussionist with a music master's degree, teaching, recording and leading an ensemble.
She uses **AI daily** and has about three months of savings, typical pay and some nearby music jobs.
She expects **arranging and editing** to lose fees before robots reach hands-on playing three years after AGI.
She tests **group teaching** with written fees, paid enrolments and sponsor funding before using her reserve.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries her most because screen-based music fees could fall faster than she can replace them.
whatWouldHelp: A **guaranteed college fee** and clear recording rights would let her shift work without risking her savings.
